title: Linux Kernel Module Load Syscall Attempts
exclusions: Detects Linux Audit `init_module` and `finit_module` syscall attempts visible to the configured audit rules. It does not detect modules built into the kernel, prove that a loaded module is malicious, cover `delete_module`, inspect module signatures or hashes, or guarantee visibility after audit tampering or loss. It is not regulatory attestation. The base search does not suppress approved activity; responders must validate any time-bound exception against change records.
evidence: When deployed, retain the version-controlled `kernel_module_load` audit rule, the `linux_kernel_module_load_syscalls` saved-search definition, dispatch and alert history, and exported result rows containing `firstTime`, `host`, `msg`, `syscall`, `module_name`, `success`, `exit`, `actor`, `comm`, and `exe`. These artefacts show collection and search operation; they do not establish that every host was continuously audited.

controlTest.positiveScenario: Index two synthetic `sourcetype=auditd` records on host `uc-1-1-21-test` with the same `msg=audit(1760000000.100:421)`: a `type=SYSCALL` record with `SYSCALL=finit_module`, `success=yes`, `exit=0`, `AUID=tester`, `comm=modprobe`, and `exe=/usr/bin/kmod`, plus a `type=KERN_MODULE` record with `name=uc_1_1_21_test`. The search must return exactly one row with syscall `finit_module` and module name `uc_1_1_21_test`.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Index a paired synthetic `type=SYSCALL` and `type=KERN_MODULE` event on host `uc-1-1-21-test` whose interpreted syscall is `delete_module`, followed by a normal `SYSCALL=execve` event. The search must return zero rows because neither record is an `init_module` or `finit_module` attempt.

dataSources: `index=os sourcetype=auditd` events from the `rlog.sh` scripted input in the Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833). The input reads `/var/log/audit/audit.log` and translates records with `ausearch`; required fields are `host`, `msg`, `type`, and interpreted `SYSCALL`, with `success`, `exit`, `AUID`/`auid`, `UID`/`uid`, `comm`, `exe`, `pid`, `ppid`, `key`, and KERN_MODULE `name` used for context when present. `os` is a local index convention, not a Splunk default.
app: Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833). Use its `rlog.sh` input and `auditd` sourcetype for this search; the add-on's separate `linux_audit` sourcetype represents the raw Linux audit log and does not guarantee the interpreted `SYSCALL` names required here.
spl:
index=os sourcetype=auditd ((type=SYSCALL (SYSCALL=init_module OR SYSCALL=finit_module)) OR type=KERN_MODULE)
| eval syscall_name=if(type="SYSCALL",lower(SYSCALL),null()), module_name=if(type="KERN_MODULE",name,null()), actor=if(type="SYSCALL",coalesce(AUID,auid),null()), effective_user=if(type="SYSCALL",coalesce(UID,uid),null())
| stats earliest(_time) as firstTime latest(_time) as lastTime values(syscall_name) as syscall values(module_name) as module_name values(success) as success values(exit) as exit values(actor) as actor values(effective_user) as effective_user values(comm) as comm values(exe) as exe values(pid) as pid values(ppid) as ppid values(key) as key by host msg
| where mvfind(syscall,"^(init_module|finit_module)$")>=0
| fillnull value="unknown" module_name success exit actor effective_user comm exe pid ppid key
| sort 0 -firstTime
description: Reports one row per Linux Audit event identifier and host when the interpreted SYSCALL record contains an `init_module` or `finit_module` attempt. The search joins any same-event KERN_MODULE record to expose the module name and preserves process, user, success, and return-code context. A saved search running over a ten-minute lookback produces a result for every matching attempt, successful or failed.
value: Detecting unexpected kernel-module attempts helps responders prevent unapproved kernel-level code and persistence from going unnoticed. The caller, module, host role, outcome, and change record improve triage, while failed calls retain evidence of probing that a success-only search would miss.
implementation: Create persistent Linux Audit exit-filter rules for `init_module` and `finit_module` on each supported host ABI, load and verify them, then enable the add-on's `rlog.sh` input into the chosen operating-system index. Confirm interpreted `SYSCALL` values and shared `msg` identifiers before saving the search. Run every five minutes over ten minutes, trigger on any result, and suppress duplicate notifications by `host,msg` rather than hiding later calls.
visualization: Show a newest-first table with `firstTime`, `host`, `syscall`, `module_name`, `success`, `exit`, `actor`, `comm`, and `exe`. Add an hourly count split by `success` and panels for modules first seen on each host or host role. Label unknown module names explicitly; absence of a KERN_MODULE record is a telemetry limitation, not proof that no module was named.
dataModelAcceleration: Not applicable. Splunk documents `auditd` as having no CIM data-model mapping for this input, and the search relies on Linux Audit event identifiers plus SYSCALL and KERN_MODULE record fields.

knownFalsePositives:
1. **Kernel or driver package maintenance** — An approved kernel update, DKMS build, or driver package can load a new module. Match the host and time to the package transaction and change ticket, then verify the installed package and module signer before closing the result.

2. **Hardware discovery and hot-plug** — `udev` or another device manager can invoke `modprobe` when a network, storage, or peripheral device appears. Confirm the corresponding device event and that the module is approved for that hardware class.

3. **Boot and service initialization** — Required filesystem, storage, networking, security, or virtualization modules may load during a normal boot or service start. Correlate with boot telemetry and the host-role baseline; a familiar module at an unusual time still requires review.

4. **Authorized administrative testing** — Platform engineers or detection testers may deliberately call `modprobe` or `insmod`. Require a named change or exercise record and compare `actor`, `comm`, `exe`, module name, and test window.

**Suppression mechanism:** if local policy permits alert-time suppression, maintain an owner-reviewed `linux_kernel_module_exceptions.csv` lookup with exact `host_role`, `module_name`, `comm`, `valid_from`, `valid_until`, `change_id`, and `owner` fields. Filter only rows inside an active approved window after the base search has been retained. Reject wildcard module names and expired or ownerless rows; never suppress all calls by root, and retain failed attempts for review.
reviewer: documentation review against primary Linux Audit, Splunk, and MITRE ATT&CK sources
detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and scope

Use a Linux kernel with the Audit subsystem enabled and an operational `auditd` service. The service account running the Splunk Universal Forwarder must be able to execute the add-on's supported `rlog.sh` input; follow the add-on's documented deployment and privilege guidance rather than replacing it with an unreviewed polling script. Deploy the Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833) to the collection tier and make its search-time knowledge available where the search runs. Create or select an operating-system event index. This catalogue calls it `os`; if the deployment uses another name, change only the index term consistently.

This control records attempts to invoke the two Linux syscalls that load modules. `init_module` loads an image supplied from memory, while `finit_module` loads from a file descriptor. It deliberately includes `success=no` because denied attempts can be investigative leads. It does not label every result malicious and does not inspect module content.

## 1. Configure persistent Linux Audit rules

Place a dedicated file such as `/etc/audit/rules.d/40-kernel-module-load.rules` under configuration management. On a 64-bit host, use one combined exit-filter rule:

```text
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S init_module -S finit_module -k kernel_module_load
```

On a bi-architecture host that permits 32-bit system calls, add the corresponding `arch=b32` rule after confirming those syscall names exist for that ABI. Linux Audit documentation recommends specifying the architecture before syscall names and using separate rules for 32-bit and 64-bit tables. Do not add an `auid` filter: kernel module operations often run through root-owned services, and filtering to interactive users would create a known blind spot.

Load the managed rule with the distribution-supported audit workflow, for example `augenrules --load`, and inspect `auditctl -l`. If the ruleset is immutable, follow the host's controlled reboot procedure instead of weakening immutability. Confirm that the effective rule contains both syscalls and the `kernel_module_load` key. Monitor audit backlog and loss separately; a search that receives no events cannot distinguish quiet hosts from failed collection.

## 2. Collect and verify the records

Enable the existing `rlog.sh` scripted-input stanza supplied by `Splunk_TA_nix` in a local configuration layer. Route it to the selected index and retain the add-on-defined `sourcetype=auditd`. Splunk documents this source type as Audit records translated by `ausearch`; that translation is important because the raw kernel record stores architecture-dependent syscall numbers while the interpreted event supplies values such as `SYSCALL=finit_module`.

Do not substitute `sourcetype=linux_audit` without rewriting and testing the search. The add-on documents that as the raw Linux audit-log source type, and raw `syscall` values can be numeric. After deployment, search the latest `auditd` events and verify `host`, `msg`, `type`, interpreted `SYSCALL`, `success`, `exit`, user identifiers, `comm`, `exe`, `pid`, `ppid`, and `key`. Where the kernel emits a KERN_MODULE auxiliary record, verify that it shares the SYSCALL record's `msg` value and exposes `name`. The shared timestamp-and-serial identifier is what lets the SPL attach the module name without `transaction`.

## 3. Save and schedule the detection

Save the catalogue SPL as `linux_kernel_module_load_syscalls`. The initial clause is fully parenthesized so both syscall alternatives remain constrained to `index=os`, `sourcetype=auditd`, and `type=SYSCALL`; the second branch admits KERN_MODULE context. This is intentional because Splunk's search command evaluates `OR` before implied `AND`, unlike `eval` and `where`. Removing the parentheses can silently widen the search.

The aggregation grain is `host,msg`, which represents one Audit event on one host. `stats` joins the SYSCALL and KERN_MODULE records and the final `where` removes unrelated KERN_MODULE records. Schedule the search every five minutes with `dispatch.earliest_time=-10m@m` and `dispatch.latest_time=@m` to tolerate modest forwarding delay. Trigger when the result count is greater than zero. To avoid repeat notifications from the overlapping window, suppress for 15 minutes on both `host` and `msg`; do not suppress only by host, because that could hide a second module-load attempt. Preserve all result rows even if notification routing is throttled.

## 4. Validate without claiming production execution

First run the positive and negative synthetic scenarios in `controlTest` through an isolated test input or a search-time fixture approved by the Splunk administrator. The positive pair must collapse to one row and carry `finit_module`, `uc_1_1_21_test`, `success=yes`, and the test actor. The paired `delete_module` event and ordinary `execve` event must produce no row. Repeat the positive test with `SYSCALL=init_module` and with `success=no`; both must remain visible.

On a disposable Linux test host, an authorized operator may exercise an approved, harmless module-load workflow and compare the indexed event with `ausearch -k kernel_module_load -i`. Record the test host, rule version, Audit event serial, Splunk search time, and expected row. This optional runtime test requires change approval and is not asserted by this documentation review.

## 5. Alert, dashboard, and respond

Route each result to the Linux security or platform-security queue with the module name, syscall, success, return code, actor, executable, PID, parent PID, host, and Audit message identifier. A failed load is not equivalent to a successful insertion, but repeated failures or an unexpected caller can still merit escalation. Dashboard counts should separate success values and should never replace unknown module names with a guessed filename.

The runbook should confirm the host and clock, retrieve all records sharing `msg`, check the corresponding change and package transactions, and identify why the caller needed `CAP_SYS_MODULE`. For successful unexpected loads, inspect `/proc/modules` or `/sys/module`, collect module path, package ownership, signer, and hash using approved response tooling, and compare with the host-role baseline. Escalate unexplained or untrusted modules under the incident-response process; do not unload a module automatically because removal can destabilize storage, networking, or security controls.

## 6. Troubleshoot and preserve evidence

No results after an approved test usually indicates a missing Audit rule, unsupported ABI rule, disabled `rlog.sh`, insufficient collector privilege, wrong index, or a sourcetype mismatch. Numeric `syscall` values with no uppercase `SYSCALL` indicate raw rather than interpreted collection. A row with `module_name=unknown` means the matching SYSCALL was present but no same-window KERN_MODULE record was available; inspect the complete Audit event before changing extraction. Duplicate alerts should be addressed with `host,msg` suppression, not `dedup host`, which discards distinct calls.

Keep the managed rule, effective-rule output, input configuration, saved-search definition, dispatch history, alert disposition, and any approved exception together under the organization's evidence-retention policy. Document collection gaps and audit loss explicitly. These records support operational review of this detection; they do not prove kernel integrity or compliance on their own.
grandmaExplanation: We watch for attempts to add powerful new parts to the heart of a Linux server. Some are normal, but an unexpected one deserves a quick check before it can hide harmful activity or take control.
